svg.aria-label: Azure Load Balancer in four bands: the five-tuple hash on the data path, what session persistence and upstream SNAT do to it, the health probe whose defaults differ by tool, and what happens when one or all instances probe down.
svg.title: A hash you do not control, and a probe whose default depends on which tool created it
svg.text: Load Balancer: the rule is the easy part
Layer 4 pass-through. Nothing is terminated or inspected. Two mechanisms decide everything: a hash, and a probe.
1 · THE DATA PATH
Frontend IP config
public → public LB
Load-balancing rule
frontend:port → backend:port
five-tuple hash, per flow
src IP · src port · dst IP · dst port · proto
Backend pool
up to 5,000
Stickiness exists only within a transport session. A new session reuses the source IP but a new source port, so it hashes elsewhere.
An inbound NAT rule is the same machinery aimed at one instance, using the same hash-based distribution.
2 · WHAT CHANGES THE HASH — AND WHAT STARVES IT
Session persistence removes inputs; it tracks nothing
None — five-tuple · loadDistribution Default
Client IP — two-tuple: src IP, dst IP · SourceIP
Client IP and protocol — three-tuple · SourceIPProtocol
An upstream firewall doing SNAT breaks distribution
Few visible source IPs, predictable source ports
→ “highly skewed or no distribution”
Happens with the default five-tuple and healthy backends.
Clients behind a proxy may be seen as one unique client. Adding or removing a backend recomputes the distribution for everyone.
The documented remedies change client counts or instance counts — not a single load balancer setting.
3 · THE PROBE DECIDES ELIGIBILITY — AND ITS DEFAULT DEPENDS ON THE TOOL
Interval default, same resource
Azure portal — 5 seconds
ARM, REST, CLI, PowerShell — 15 seconds (min 5)
Three times slower to notice a failure, set by nobody.
Threshold means two different things
TCP — consecutive successes and failures both honoured
HTTP — any explicit 200 / non-200 acts immediately
so the threshold damps silence, never a 500.
HTTP/S timeout is fixed at 30 seconds whatever the interval — six intervals at the portal default. TCP probes have no separate timeout.
Source is 168.63.129.16 for IPv4, a link-local address for IPv6, permitted by the AzureLoadBalancer service tag by default.
Probe validation runs only in the portal; PowerShell, CLI, templates and the API do not require or check a probe definition.
Never probe a port an appliance proxies: one backend’s blip marks down the appliance fronting the whole pool.
4 · WHAT A FAILED PROBE ACTUALLY DOES
One instance down
New TCP connections go to the healthy ones
Established TCP to the failed one continues; UDP moves
All instances down — Standard
No new flows enter the pool
Established TCP continues; all UDP terminates
The retired Basic SKU killed every TCP flow when all probes were down. That is the largest behavioural difference between them.
The probe governs admission, not eviction: a failing instance keeps serving every connection it already holds.
Basic Load Balancer was retired on 30 September 2025. Two SKUs remain: Standard, and Gateway for appliance chaining.
A listening socket proves a port is open. It proves nothing about whether the thing behind it can answer.
